cards.front: Recall a key point about Developing and Communicating Ideas
cards.back: Freehand sketching: quick, expressive, captures ideas rapidly - the primary tool for initial concept generation. Annotations explain function, materials and dimensions.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developing and Communicating Ideas
cards.back: Rendering: adding tone, texture and colour to sketches - creates realistic appearance, shows material properties, communicates design intent to clients.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developing and Communicating Ideas
cards.back: CAD (Computer-Aided Design): 2D (vector for laser cutting), 3D (solid modelling for visualisation, FEA, 3D printing). Precision, easy modification, virtual testing, output for CAM.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developing and Communicating Ideas
cards.back: Orthographic projection: 2D technical drawings showing front, side and plan views - precise, scaled, used for manufacture. Third-angle projection (UK standard).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Developing and Communicating Ideas
cards.back: Exploded views: show how components fit together - parts separated along assembly axes with lines showing connections. Essential for assembly instructions.

cards.front: What should you know about d&t exam tips?
cards.back: For communication questions: 1) Name the drawing/technique, 2) Describe its features, 3) Explain its purpose, 4) Compare with alternatives, 5) Justify its use for the specific context.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: CAD has replaced sketching because it is more precise and professional, so sketching is no longer important. Correct: CAD and sketching are complementary, not competing. Sketching excels at rapid concept generation. CAD excels at precision, modification, virtual testing and manufacturing output.
